content: Gramicidin is a complex mixture of six antibiotic compounds, primarily consisting of Gramicidins A, B, and C, which account for approximately 80%, 6%, and 14% of the mixture, respectively. These compounds are derived from the soil bacterium Bacillus brevis and are collectively referred to as Gramicidin D. Structurally, Gramicidin D is a linear pentadecapeptide, meaning it is composed of a chain of 15 amino acids. This linear structure contrasts with Gramicidin S, which is a cyclic peptide. Gramicidin exhibits antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive bacteria, with the exception of Gram-positive bacilli, and is also effective against certain Gram-negative organisms, such as Neisseria species. However, its therapeutic use is restricted to topical applications because it causes hemolysis (destruction of red blood cells) at concentrations lower than those required to kill bacterial cells, making it unsuitable for systemic administration. The outermost layer of the skin, the epidermis, is composed of dead cells, which prevents harm when Gramicidin is applied topically. It is primarily used as a topical antibiotic and is one of the three active ingredients in the consumer antibiotic product Neosporin Ophthalmic Solution. In 1939, the French-American microbiologist René Dubos isolated a substance called tyrocidine, which he later demonstrated to be composed of two components: Gramicidin (20%) and Tyrocidine (80%). These were among the first antibiotics to be produced commercially. Composition and Structure Gramicidin has a general molecular formula: formyl-L-X-Gly-L-Ala-D-Leu-L-Ala-D-Val-L-Val-D-Val-L-Trp-D-Leu-L-Y-D-Leu-L-Trp-D-Leu-L-Trp-ethanolamine. The variables X and Y depend on the specific Gramicidin molecule. Variants of Gramicidin exist with either valine or isoleucine at the X position. The Y position determines the specific type of Gramicidin: Gramicidin A contains tryptophan, Gramicidin B contains phenylalanine, and Gramicidin C contains tyrosine. The alternating stereochemical configurations (D and L forms) of the amino acids are critical for the formation of the β-helix structure. The peptide chain assembles within the hydrophobic interior of the cellular lipid bilayer to form a β-helix. This helix is not long enough to span the entire membrane, so two helices dimerize in a head-to-head configuration to create an elongated channel that spans the membrane. The structure of the Gramicidin dimer in micelles and lipid bilayers has been elucidated using solution and solid-state NMR techniques. In organic solvents and crystals, Gramicidin forms non-native double helices. Function as an Ion Channel Gramicidin D functions as an ion channel, as demonstrated by Hladky and Haydon, who studied its unit conductance properties. These channels are highly selective for monovalent cations, and their single-channel conductance for alkali cations follows the same order as the aqueous mobilities of these ions. Divalent cations, such as Ca²⁺, block the channel by binding near its entrance, rendering it essentially impermeable to divalent cations. The channel also excludes anions, particularly Cl⁻, due to the thermodynamic stability of its hydration shell, which is stronger than that of most monovalent cations. The Gramicidin channel is permeable to most monovalent cations, which pass through the channel in single file. The channel contains approximately six water molecules, nearly all of which must be displaced when an ion is transported. As ions move through the Gramicidin pore, they carry along a single file of water molecules, a phenomenon known as flux coupling. In the presence of a second type of permeable ion, the fluxes of the two ions can become coupled as well. Like Valinomycin and Nonactin, the Gramicidin channel exhibits a slight preference for potassium (K⁺) over sodium (Na⁺). While it is generally impermeable to anions, under certain conditions, limited anion permeation may be observed. The ability of Gramicidin to bind and transport cations is attributed to the presence of specific cation-binding sites within the channel. Notably, there are two such binding sites: one with strong affinity and the other with weaker affinity.
